# Canvas layout hint

When the Labs canvas is on, a piece that belongs to a set can say where it goes. The hint is
optional and harmless otherwise. Pass it as `--canvas '<json>'` on `voyager files present` and
`voyager models run`, or as `canvas` in `media_command`. Single pieces need none, and it is ignored
with `--deliverable none`.

| Field            | Meaning                                                                                                                |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `group.key`      | Stable id of the section (≤ 80 chars), such as `characters`; rows sharing a key sit together.                          |
| `group.title`    | The section label (≤ 120 chars).                                                                                       |
| `group.order`    | Story order of sections, top to bottom.                                                                                |
| `group.parent`   | A group key to nest under; one level only.                                                                             |
| `group.layout`   | `"row"` (versions left to right), `"strip"` (shots in cut order) or `{"grid":{"columns","rowLabels","columnLabels"}}`. |
| `group.expected` | 1 to 64: reserves empty slots and shows "3 of 8". Slots drop when no job for the group is running.                     |
| `role`           | `reference`, `take`, `shot` or `final`: sets tile size and default section order.                                      |
| `slot`           | An index (strip, row) or `{row, column}` (grid).                                                                       |
| `pick`           | `true` on a version of the same deliverable: marks the chosen take.                                                    |

Rules:

- The user's arrangement wins. Never re-send a hint to move a row the user placed or ordered.
- Send `expected` on the first job of a set, and send the same group on every member.
- Keep group keys stable across the project; reuse a key rather than inventing a near copy.
- Set `pick` only when the user chose ("go with take 2"). A pick the user made cannot be overridden.
- Bad fields are dropped, not errors; a result saying `canvasHint: "partly ignored"` means fix
  the hint next time. Identical prompts for different slots are separate jobs.

## Examples

Character sheet, a grid of four characters by two angles. Send the same group on all eight jobs.

```sh
voyager models run … --canvas '{"group":{"key":"characters","title":"Characters","order":1,
  "layout":{"grid":{"columns":4,"columnLabels":["Mara","Theo","Ines","Bo"],
  "rowLabels":["Front","Side"]}},"expected":8},"role":"reference","slot":{"row":0,"column":2}}'
```

Storyboard, six shots in cut order. Each frame is its own deliverable, with `slot` as its index.

```sh
voyager files present shot-3.png --deliverable "Shot 3" \
  --canvas '{"group":{"key":"match-night","title":"Match night","order":3,
  "layout":"strip","expected":6},"role":"shot","slot":2}'
```

Pick, after the user chooses among takes of "Shot 3": present the chosen take again.

```sh
voyager files present takes/shot-3-take-02.mp4 --deliverable "Shot 3" --canvas '{"pick":true}'
```

# Keeping shots in one world

Shots generated one at a time drift apart. What holds them together:

- **People and recurring props are project Elements.** Reuse a fitting card or make one
  with `voyager cast create`: front, three-quarter and profile portraits (the clearest front
  as the hero), a full-body image and a short description of what stays true in every look
  (face, hair, build, wardrobe; never the medium). For
  photoreal drama, prompt the hero as "a photo of an actor" on plain grey, not a
  "character sheet" (stiff CG); full turnarounds can make a model duplicate the character.
  Put every photo the user supplies on the card (up to 64, the clearest front portrait as
  hero); a real person's likeness comes only from their photos. Props and products go
  alone on a plain background, from the user's photos when they have them. `voyager cast
  from-model` makes a card from a `.glb`.
- **Show the set on the canvas**: character references, previs frames ("Shot 1"…) and takes carry a
  canvas hint with a stable group key, as [canvas-layout](canvas-layout.md) describes.
- **Pass `cast` with the element IDs and the project directory on every image and video
  estimate and run that shows them**, retakes included. Voyager attaches the photos and
  returns each one's label; write each visible element's identity using those labels.
  `voyager cast models` lists which routes take a card's references; `voyager cast check`
  is a paid second opinion on a still's likeness; never claim a match nobody checked.
- **A model that takes only a first frame** (Kling 3.0 on Higgsfield, any image-to-video
  without a reference list) keeps the Elements from that frame: make the keyframe still with
  `cast`, then run the video with that still in the model's start-image field (`image_url`,
  `start_image_url` or `start_image`, as `voyager models show` names it) and the same `cast`.
  Voyager records the Elements and their descriptions and attaches no photos.
- **Places** come from one design: an empty location reference in the look, showing the
  place's layout and depth, with no people. Cite it as the place's design and geography,
  never its framing or first frame.
- **The scene state** changes only when the story changes it: who sits or stands where,
  relative to the set piece and each other;
  set pieces, their state and props; the light; the side of the 180° line the camera keeps
  to. Open each prompt with its part of that state, and check reverses against it: what a
  viewer reads beats any camera geometry that explains a flip away.
- **An occupied scene anchor and named setups**: once a scene's people are placed, one
  frame with everyone at their marks and scale, and the camera setups the scene reuses
  (the wide, each over-the-shoulder, each close-up), so later shots come from the same
  coverage.
- **The subject the audience follows is unmistakable** in every shot: a colour or
  silhouette nothing else in the frame shares, described the same way in every prompt, so wides and overheads
  still read.
- **Each shot's entry and exit state**: what has happened by its end, which take is the approved one, and which later shots were made from
  it, so a correction is carried to everything downstream.
- **One style key** (a frame and a few words) carries the look across every prompt, and it
  wins over a photo reference: a frame drifting toward a photo's realism is a failed take.
- **Compare before spending on motion**: previs frames or a scene's draft takes,
  side by side in cut order as a script supervisor would: someone appearing, vanishing or changing seat or side, a prop gone or
  moved, a changed set piece, an angle that can't be the same place, a flipped eyeline.

Between two shots, the viewer either sees a cut or the same shot continues; a model's
duration limit decides where a generation ends, never where a shot ends.

- **Across a cut, carry the state, not the frame**: generate the next shot from its own
  references with the changed state in words. The previous shot's last frame drags its composition into the new angle.
- **Across a continuation, carry the motion**, in this order: one longer generation; the
  model's own extension (Seedance 2.5; Veo 3.1 for Veo-made clips), joined with an
  untrimmed straight cut; the kept take's last seconds as a video reference. A continuation's prompt opens on the
  action already under way, with no one entering
  who is already in frame.
- **A move through several places** is built from segments joined inside a place, never at
  a crossing. Write each change of
  place as the camera's path, not speed verbs whose blur hides a scene swap. Check each
  segment before extending from it, and retake only the one that fails.

# Kling 4.0 (and 3.0 motion control)

Evidence as of November 2026: third (8.34/10) in Curious Refuge's ten-model test of Nov 2;
not yet on Artificial Analysis. Head-to-head reviews split: Kling led on physical interaction
in one ten-test comparison (cellcog), while others gave Seedance 2.5 the edge on fight rhythm,
motion transfer and lip-sync to a supplied voice. A four-keyframe practitioner demo worked;
reliable use of all ten keyframes is unproven.

## When to choose it

- Physical action and contact; a move pinned at several moments (up to ten keyframes across
  3–30 s); Elements with voices (up to three); cheaper than Seedance at 1080p; 21:9.
- After Seedance refuses realistic faces.
- **Not:** close dialogue where faces and hands must hold, until a test shot shows they do.

Endpoints: `kling/v4/text-to-video`, `/image-to-video`, `/reference-to-video`. Modes
(Keyframes, Omni references, multi-shot) don't all combine: check `voyager models show
MODEL --json` before planning assets. The catalog has no v4 motion-control route; for
transferring one performer's motion, use Kling 3.0 motion control.

## Prompt structure

- On `kling/v4/reference-to-video`, `cast` maps people to `@Element1`, `@Element2`;
  `start_image_url` supplies an approved wide; `multi_prompt` is a list of shots, each a
  `prompt` and an integer `duration` (no `shot_type` or `generate_audio`).
- Keep each element at its mark in every shot's prompt; write "No background music."
- With keyframes, pilot two or three milestone frames first and check the contact and
  object state between them, not only the endpoints.

## Kling 3.0 and O3

Fal's `o3` is 3.0 Omni. Direct multi-shot with `multi_prompt`. References are `@Image1` and
`@Element1`. Dialogue: one label and voice per speaker, the action before the line, a linking
word between turns (`[Character A: name, voice]: "…" Immediately, [Character B: …]`), lowercase English on fal. O3 generation defaults to no audio, and O3 edit
and video-reference generation make no new sound (`keep_audio` keeps the source's). For a fixed
voice, create one (`fal-ai/kling-video/create-voice`) and bind it to the element; don't use
native `<<<voice_1>>>` tokens on fal. Only v3 has a `negative_prompt`.

## Failure modes

- A requested dolly can come back as a zoom: check near and far objects for real parallax.
- Faces and hands drift in close two-person dialogue.
- Mode combinations that look allowed can be refused or ignored; read the live schema.

# MiniMax H3, H3 Max and H3 Max Turbo

Evidence as of November 2026: H3 (768p) third in Artificial Analysis text-to-video votes and
fourth in image-to-video, at a small fraction of Seedance's price; sixth (7.83/10) in Curious
Refuge's ten-model test of Nov 2. A 99-clip blind local test (Stuubzzz, Nov 1) favoured H3 for
two-person dialogue. Practitioners use it for micro-dramas and to preview shots before a Seedance render (about
40 s per take against about two minutes for Seedance's draft mode); the Seedance render is a
new take, not a finish of the H3 one.

## When to choose it

- The cheapest credible take; fast iteration; faces and dialogue to camera; lip-sync;
  previewing shots for another model.
- H3 Max for references (up to nine Elements) and 3D-to-video from a grey-box clip. H3 Max
  Turbo is cheaper but takes only text or a start and end frame: no Elements, no video input.
- **Not:** the hero shot of a high-stakes piece when Seedance's quality is affordable.

Endpoints include `minimax/h3/…`, `minimax/h3-max/text-to-video`, `/image-to-video`,
`/reference-to-video`, `/lip-sync/image-to-video`, `/extend-video`, `/3d-to-video` and
editing tasks, and `minimax/h3-max-turbo/text-to-video` and `/image-to-video`. 1080P and Turbo run on fal, not Higgsfield.
Reference inputs can add to the bill: check `voyager models estimate`.

## Prompt structure

- On fal cite `Image 1`, `Video 1`, `Audio 1`, not `<Picture 1>`. Keep prompt fields compact
  and task-specific.
- `prompt_expansion_mode` `disabled` sends your prose unchanged; the other modes rewrite it.
- The labelled format puts the picture in `integrated_multimodal_description:` with
  `[Shot 2] At 00:03.500, the camera cuts to …` and camera as type, amplitude and speed
  ("pushes in with small amplitude at slow speed"); ambience in `overall_soundscape:`; score in
  `non_diegetic_music:`, where `N/A` means no music.
- Speakers get IDs, `(S1)`, and lines go in `<d>[English] exact words</d>`.
- Reference mode: an image cited inside a `<Subject N>` definition supplies that subject; a
  standalone image becomes a target frame whose viewpoint the take copies.
- `target_audio_url` replaces the whole soundtrack. A video reference's sound is not a voice
  reference: bind a voice once, and when its original sound leaks, set `retention_analysis` to
  `reference`, not `fully_copy`.

## Failure modes

- Extending a speaking character from first/last frames loses the voice; extend in reference
  mode with the voice bound.
- Some H3 Max takes open squashed (`voyager media review` flags it; trim the frames it names),
  and H3 Max runs slightly longer than requested; trim to length.
- A blocking puppet can render as a puppet when its clip is the motion reference.
- Check captions and speech timing across the whole clip, not just the opening.

# Other video models and routes

For when a shot needs what one of these uniquely does, or the user names it. Evidence as of
November 2026.

## FLUX 3 Max

Fourth in Artificial Analysis text-to-video votes; twelfth in image-to-video. Fast
text-to-video; its launch discount ends November 7, after which it costs more than Wan or
Kling at 720p. One flowing paragraph for a single take, sound last; several shots as
`SHOT ONE: … HARD CUT. SHOT TWO: …`. Its default high `reasoning_level` can add a cut to a single shot; `low` makes
that less likely. An off-screen line needs a `voiceover` cue, or it may be drawn as text.
Keyframes-to-video takes frame-indexed anchors.

## HeyGen Video 1

Ranks near the top of Artificial Analysis votes at a low listed price; independent quality
evidence is still thin. A candidate for low budgets.

## Veo 3.1

Short talking-person setups and extending a Veo clip. One focused moment per clip; for
image-to-video, describe only motion and camera. Speech goes after a colon without quotes
(`… says: …`), since quotes can render as text.
`negative_prompt` takes nouns; reference-to-video has no negative field and no label syntax.
Timestamped beats (`[00:00-00:02] …`) suit two to four shots of one scene. A voice carries
through an extension only if audible in the last second. `auto_fix` rewrites a prompt that
fails policy, so a changed result may not reflect your prompt.

## Gemini Omni Flash 1.1

Short speech and edits; renders legible text. It cuts between shots unless told "single continuous shot, no scene cuts", and
picks its own soundtrack unless you describe one. No negative field: write "No dialogue. No
background music." Speech after a colon, unquoted. References bind as `<IMAGE_REF_0>` from
zero. Edits are short and end "Keep everything else the same." It ignores the audio in video
references.

## LTX 2.5

Higher resolution and frame rates, audio-driven scenes, one speaker or a camera orbit; it can
repeat a two-person exchange, so use H3 or Seedance for those. Flowing prose for simple shots,
screenplay style for dialogue; write "a beat of silence" or set the duration, since it adds no
pauses. `voyager models show lightricks/ltx-2.5/text-to-video/fast --json` lists combinations.

## Local models

`voyager models list local --json`: free on this computer and slower; tell the user up front
and keep talking while it runs. Remove a conflicting provider pin, or use a model's
`hostedAlternative` ID to estimate a hosted run.

## Supplied footage and people

A portrait plus speech (Sync v3 avatar, H3 Max lip-sync, HeyGen Avatar 5); new speech in
footage (Sync v3 lip-sync); a performance onto a character (Kling 3.0 motion control); a
masked region replaced (Wan VACE inpainting, which brings the original back unless that area
is greyed out first or `preprocess` is on); upscaling (Topaz, SeedVR; test a short section
first).

## Provider keys

A Runway API key runs Runway's own models as `runway:<model>/<operation>`, only on that key and
never as a fallback. A BytePlus ModelArk key, once enabled in Connectors → Providers, runs
Seedance and Seedream natively as `byteplus:<model-id>`; fal requests don't translate to it,
its dollar price is unknown, it can't upload local videos, and a lost task ID leaves the job
uncertain: never replay it. A personal OpenAI key opens no video route.

# Seedance 2.5 and 2.0

Evidence as of November 2026: Seedance 2.5 ranked first overall (8.94/10) and 2.0 second
(8.40, ahead of 2.5 on prompt adherence) in Curious Refuge's ten-model test of Nov 2;
2.5 leads Artificial Analysis image-to-video votes. Each model's playbook is its own: never
copy this syntax into another model's prompt.

## When to choose it

- **2.5:** the scene's people and place must hold across cuts; many references (up to 30
  images, plus video and audio references); multi-shot scenes up to 30 s; editing or
  extending a clip; the hero shots of a piece.
- **2.0:** only when the user names it. It costs about two thirds of 2.5 for slightly lower
  quality, and lost both of our blind side-by-side comparisons with 2.5; for a cheaper take,
  H3 or Wan cost about a fifth.
- **Not:** a long piece on a tight budget (draft cheaply or mix models), or realistic faces
  where the route refuses them (below).

Endpoints include `bytedance/seedance-2.5/reference-to-video`, `/image-to-video`,
`/text-to-video`, `/draft/complete` and `/us/…` variants, and `bytedance/seedance-2.0/…`.
`voyager models show MODEL --json` lists live limits, draft resolutions and completion rules.

## Prompt structure

- For Seedance, always state length and aspect ratio. Use auto aspect only when matching a source image.
- On fal write `@Image1`, `@Video1`, `@Audio1` by position in each list. Upload subjects in
  order of first appearance, or it swaps characters, and define each once.
- ByteDance's guide orders a prompt as asset mapping, a summary sentence, beats as whole-second ranges
  (`0-3 seconds: …`), then what stays constant. Fractions or gaps in the ranges confuse it, and
  timestamps guide pacing rather than set frame-exact cuts.
- Dialogue in `{}` after its language (`says in English {…}`), effects in `< >`, music in
  `()`.
- The `task` (reference, editing, extension) must match the prompt: "Strictly edit @Video1:
  from 4-6 seconds, change …; leave the rest unchanged", "Extend @Video1 forward", never
  "reference @Video1" for those. After an edit, check outside the interval too and re-measure
  the duration.
- Stubborn music needs an audio policy, repeated per shot, naming the excluded forms (score,
  melody, synth, drone, stinger). In long takes, repeat two or three fixed identifiers at later
  beats. Intense emotion words can make eyes glow ("normal human eyes").
- An audio edit re-renders the picture and can shorten it by about 0.4 s: for an audio-only
  change, compare against the original and keep its picture if that's better.
- Known fixes: remove subtitles from a reference video, since they override a subtitle ban;
  reword water, wave or echo words when they bring bubbling or whistling; for a mixed-language
  edit, give the full timed target script with every line translated.

## Draft, then finish

Seedance's draft mode renders a cheap 480p take; `draft/complete` finishes that same take at
full resolution, keeping its camera and performance. In a controlled test it cost about the
same as drafting on H3 Max and rendering on Seedance, with better drafts. Keep the draft's
ID and its completion deadline (hosts differ; check the live schema rather than assuming a
number of days). Image-to-video and draft completion may come back unpriced in Voyager: say
the price is unknown and get the user's OK before running it.

## Faces

With photoreal Elements on Voyager credits, Ultra and GigaMax keep a real draft that
`draft/complete` can finish, falling back to another host when the first refuses the face;
lower plans are refused before anything is sent, and a final refusal can still happen. Own-key
routes follow their provider. On a refusal never resend: offer the error's named models
(H3 / H3 Max, Kling 4.0), a stylized Element or no face reference.

## Voices and native speech

Reusing the same reference images keeps a character's voice the same across generations (one
filmmaker's report on Seedance 2.5, Nov 2026, who saw the same on Veo 3). Native speech can
garble a word or mispronounce a name: patch that word in the edit or re-voice the line, and
have a native speaker check lines in other languages.

## Failure modes

- Staging inside a multi-shot take can reset between shots (an approach skipped, someone back
  at their first mark): replace the shot with a separately generated insert.
- Strong reference adherence also copies a reference's flaws and composition.
- Identity holds better than physical contact: hands touching, objects changing hands and
  collisions need checking at normal speed.

# Wan 3.0

Evidence as of November 2026: first in Artificial Analysis text-to-video votes, ninth in
image-to-video; fifth (7.98/10) in Curious Refuge's ten-model test of Nov 2. A 49-run test
against Seedance 2.0 found Wan holds the input image, identity through motion and physics
better, while Seedance 2.0 leads on multi-subject interaction and style (vendor test, Atlas
Cloud). ClipRush's counted review (Oct 20) found strong dialogue and reference fidelity,
with animals drifting and cuts it wasn't asked for.

## When to choose it

- One continuous take up to 30 s at native 1080p; a scene from text alone; product clips and
  briefs built from a document or page; fast, cheap drafts (480p is a small fraction of
  Seedance's price).
- **Not:** several characters interacting closely (Seedance), editing or extending a clip (no
  fal edit or extend endpoint), or animals that must stay the same.

Endpoints: `alibaba/wan-3.0/text-to-video`, `/image-to-video`, `/reference-to-video`, and
`alibaba/wan-3.0-prime/…` (pick Prime when its measured waiting time is the better trade).
`voyager models show alibaba/wan-3.0/reference-to-video --json` lists reference combinations
(up to 10 images; video and audio references capped together), duration caps and input
billing.

## Prompt structure

- "One continuous shot" on the first line for a single take; "hard cut" or "dissolve" between
  shots. It cuts on its own otherwise, so check the midpoint for an unwanted cut.
- `Image N`, `Video N`, `Audio N` are numbered separately and bind by order; scope each to what it
  supplies, and say which image is which
  character.
- Write "No dialogue." when nobody speaks, or it adds some.
- Plan a long take as stages with end states the model can aim at; one clear action per stage.
- End with "Negative prompt list:" naming only unwanted items.
- Prompt expansion is on by default and rewrites your prose. For an exact shot list or verbatim
  dialogue, turn it off and compare; record which setting each take used.
- Describe the camera's motion directly.

## Failure modes

- Unrequested cuts mid-take; dialogue added to silent shots.
- Animals and small labels drift; check spelling on any visible lettering.
- A failed stretch of a long take: regenerate a shorter insert rather than the whole take.

## Watch and listen to a clip

Use this only when the task needs evidence beyond local technical checks.

| Question | Approach |
| --- | --- |
| Layout, text, framing or a still | Extract a labelled contact sheet and inspect it: `voyager media frames clip.mp4 --output review/frames-v1 --times '[0,2,4,6,8,10,12]'`. |
| Loudness, black frames, silence or duration | `voyager media review clip.mp4 --json` measures the file locally; it does not watch motion or listen to the soundtrack. |
| What was said | `voyager speech transcribe clip.mp4 --local --output transcript-v1` writes word timings locally. A transcript does not establish tone, music, SFX or lip-sync. |
| Fine motion: lip sync, mouth shapes, hands, small text | A hosted review sees about one frame a second (its job's `coverage` says so); if appropriate, check locally with a dense strip: `voyager media frames clip.mp4 --output review/lips-v1 --around '[3.2]' --window 1 --step 0.04`, adding `--crop` for the face. |
| Motion over time, audio/video sync, or how music, voice and SFX sound | Ask a video+audio understanding model through `voyager models run`, as below. This is a paid upload. |

For an audio-only recording, make a small temporary MP4 with a static picture and
its original audio, then use that clip.

### Hosted understanding

The outer `model` is a fal endpoint; the downstream model belongs in native `input`.
The downstream Google name does not choose Google-key billing. Check the live schema
with `voyager models show openrouter/router/video --refresh --json` and inspect
`voyager models estimate --input @.voyager/request.json --json` before spending. A null
estimate means unknown cost, not free.

Save this with your other working files as `.voyager/request.json`; a relative `$file` path
would resolve from that folder, so name the video by its absolute path:

```json
{
  "model": "openrouter/router/video",
  "input": {
    "model": "google/gemini-3.8-flash",
    "video_urls": [{ "$file": "/absolute/project/exports/demo.mp4" }],
    "prompt": "Describe the motion and what you hear, including music, voice and SFX. Is the sound synchronized with the picture? Give approximate times and distinguish observations from uncertainty.",
    "reasoning": true,
    "max_tokens": 1500
  }
}
```

```sh
voyager models estimate --input @.voyager/request.json --json
voyager models run --input @.voyager/request.json --json
voyager jobs wait JOB_ID --timeout 60 --json
voyager jobs result JOB_ID --json
```

Read the returned JSON result file's `output` and `usage`, and the job's `coverage.summary`:
how many frames the model saw, how far apart and at what detail.

### Billing and limits

**Verified October 15, 2026:** `openrouter/router/video` with
`google/gemini-3.8-flash` works on **Voyager credits without a personal fal key**,
and on the user's own **FAL key**. Voyager's provider order chooses the payer;
the downstream model does not require the user's Google or OpenRouter key.
Read the estimate's `payer`, `billing` and `route` and the job's actual `served`
connection.

Prefer one clip per request
when source identity matters. Keep `reasoning: true` for this
model.

Voyager allows up to 512 MiB per file, but the endpoint can impose less: a large upload can
succeed and still fail at inference on a downstream limit on the expanded request, so send a
short or compressed clip. Do not assume native
Google sampling or processing controls exist in the router's schema.

---
name: make-ai-video
description: "Generate video shots, ads and commercials from prompts or images, or restyle existing footage with Voyager models; storyboard and assemble films."
applications:
  - id: moda
    role: primary
  - id: blender
    role: alternative
  - id: resolve
    role: alternative
  - id: ffmpeg
    role: fallback
  - id: remotion
    role: alternative
voyager:
  schemaVersion: 1
  design: optional
---

## What this skill is for

Generated video, from single shots, ads and social clips to story films, and restyled
footage the user supplies. Captured-room tours start in
[room-to-video](../room-to-video/SKILL.md), software demos in
[make-product-demo](../make-product-demo/SKILL.md) (models garble interface text, so real
screens come from real recordings), animated type and graphics in
[make-motion-graphics](../make-motion-graphics/SKILL.md), and cutting footage the user
already has in [edit-video](../edit-video/SKILL.md).

The work has two halves. First you find the film the user has in mind; then you make it,
which is where model choice, references, previs and prompting matter. Keep the second half
out of the first: the user hears about models and techniques only when they want a say, or
when a choice changes the cost or what they'll see.

## Working with the user

The user is the director: the film in their head is the one you're making, and they have
the final say. You're the experienced crew beside them. You bring the craft, propose
concrete ideas, make the work, and say when a choice costs money or quality. Whatever they
haven't decided, you propose, as a proposal that's easy to change.

People show what they want more readily by reacting than by answering. A short pitch (what
happens, the feel, who's in it, roughly how long), with pictures where the look is open, draws
out what they picture; a list of questions mostly draws out guesses.

The user sees only what you write in a message or a question, not the plan in your notes: a
story they never saw is yours, not theirs. A choice between concrete options, such as look
frames or endings, is easiest to answer on a question card with each picture on its own option,
so the label and the image can't come apart.

Ask about what only they can know, such as who it's for or a moment they're already picturing,
not about what you can infer or decide. Before committing the whole piece, test what's
uncertain: look frames when the look is open, a test shot or a draft scene when the approach is
untried.

A short or vague brief says little about the person: a busy cinematographer and a
first-timer can write the same line. Name the real choices in plain words, with the
technical term beside them where it helps, so someone with opinions can take hold of them
and someone without can read past. How they respond tells you what they want to steer and how
much to show them for the rest of the conversation.

A script, shot list or choice they name (a model, editor, length) is carried out as given,
with your expertise as brief notes beside it. A length they name is the length you
deliver; add beats, or say why you'd go shorter. "Just make it" means they trust your
choices: make one strong version and show it.

## Choosing models

A BytePlus ModelArk key is enabled in Apps & Models → Providers.

Pick the model from what each shot needs, then from the budget. Seedance 2.5 gives the best
finished shots. H3 and Wan are close behind on quality at a third to a fifth of its price,
depending on the route; a model at two thirds of the price for slightly less quality
(Seedance 2.0) is rarely a trade worth making. For a simple shot the cheaper tier often looks
the same; for a hard one Seedance's quality saves retakes. No model leads at everything, rankings move every few weeks, and a piece often uses two: a cheap model or a
draft mode to find the take, and a stronger one for the takes you keep. Read the chosen
model's playbook before its first prompt; it holds the inputs, prompt structure and known
failures that make the difference.

The frontier as of November 2026, from blind leaderboards, independent tests and
practitioners' reports (each playbook cites its evidence):

| Model | Where it leads | Watch for | Playbook |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Seedance 2.5** | Best overall in independent tests and image-to-video votes; most references (up to 30 images), multi-shot scenes with timed cuts, editing and extending footage, draft then finish the same take | The most expensive; refuses realistic faces on some routes and plans | [seedance](references/models/seedance.md) |
| **Wan 3.0** | Top of text-to-video votes; native 30 s single takes at 1080p; holds the input image and physics; a fraction of Seedance's price | Adds cuts and dialogue unless told not to; animals drift | [wan](references/models/wan.md) |
| **Kling 4.0** | Physical action and contact; up to ten keyframes across a 30 s take; Elements with voices | Faces and hands in close dialogue; mixed reports overall | [kling](references/models/kling.md) |
| **MiniMax H3 / H3 Max** | Near the top of both leaderboards at a small fraction of Seedance's price; fast; faces, dialogue and lip-sync; Turbo for the cheapest drafts | Speech timing and captions across the full clip; voice changes when extending from frames | [minimax-h3](references/models/minimax-h3.md) |
| **FLUX 3 Max** | Fast, strong text-to-video | Weaker from a start image; can add a cut | [others](references/models/others.md) |

Others (Seedance 2.0, Veo 3.1, Gemini Omni Flash 1.1, LTX 2.5, HeyGen Video 1, Kling 3.0
motion control) are in [others](references/models/others.md) or their playbooks, for
when a shot needs what they uniquely do or the user names them.

How the needs map, as a starting point rather than a rule:

- **People who recur across shots, several characters, a cast held through a scene:**
  Seedance 2.5 from references; H3 Max or Kling 4.0 when the budget is tight or Seedance
  refuses the faces.
- **One long continuous take, a product, a scene from text alone:** Wan 3.0.
- **Physical action, contact, a move pinned at several moments:** Kling 4.0, piloted on the
  hard beat first.
- **Dialogue to camera, fast iteration, the cheapest credible take:** H3 / H3 Max.
- **Editing or extending a clip, restyling footage, finishing an animatic:** Seedance 2.5's
  editing and extension; H3 Max 3D-to-video for a grey-box source.

**Budget.** Before the first paid work, price the whole piece with `voyager models
estimate` on representative requests, never from memory or a list price, and give it in the
plan with who pays. Plan for retakes: practitioners keep roughly one take in three or four
for ordinary shots and far fewer for hard physics, hands, multi-person blocking or dialogue.
Drafting first saves most of the cost: in a controlled test, drafting a scene first, in
Seedance's own draft mode or on H3 Max, cost about a third of rendering it straight in
Seedance. Seedance's own draft keeps the take's camera and
performance when finished, so prefer it when Seedance is the finish. For a long piece on a
small budget, most of the runtime can be stills with camera moves and a few generated hero
shots.

Keep one scene on one model where you can, so its look holds; across models, share the same
references and style key and grade the cut as one. `voyager models list --kind video
--json` covers models this file doesn't name; `voyager models show MODEL --json` gives the
live inputs and limits, and where they disagree with this file, they win.

## Making it

Plan a scene the way an editor would cut it. A brief names destinations; the scene is the beats between them, with the turning
points shown and the dull middle skipped. Each shot opens before its key action, because a
shot that opens on the result has nothing left to do, and the brief's last action usually
deserves room to finish before the cut. Write the shot list one line per shot: what we see,
size and angle, the camera's move, duration, sound, and for anything that moves across cuts,
which way it travels on screen and what it's heading toward. A model left to choose picks a new
direction each shot.

**References first.** References carry identity and look; the prompt carries action and
camera. People and props that recur hold best as
[Elements](references/keeping-shots-in-one-world.md), a place that recurs as one location
reference, and the look as one style key; make what the piece's shots actually show, since a
product on a plain background needs no room and a face-only presenter no full-body view. A start frame
earns its place when it is the user's image, a frame restyled from previs to pin the
layout, or an exact opening composition the shot depends on. A still made only to start a
shot hands the video its flaws and its "generated still" look: the model copies the frame's
composition and errors into every second. Chaining clips through their last frames drifts
further each time.

**Scenes as one generation.** People, light and room hold together best inside one
multi-shot generation with timed hard cuts. An occupied anchor, one still with everyone at
their marks, passed as a reference, keeps the room the same room. Treat the result as
coverage: when one shot inside it fails, generate that shot alone as an insert and splice
it in, since a time-ranged edit barely changes staging.

**Previs** is a quick Blender grey-box of the set, the people as plain proxies at their marks
and a camera per setup, rendered as stills or a short animatic
([Blender's previs execution](../blender/SKILL.md#previs-execution)). Its value is easy
to underrate from the prompt side, because a prompt that states positions reads as complete.
The takes are where staging falls apart: people swap sides across a reverse, the 180° line
flips between cuts, a camera move wanders, an action misses its mark, the room rearranges
itself. A scene with several cuts of the same people, movement through space or a planned
camera move usually needs one, and it costs minutes of agent time and no generation spend,
against retakes that cost both. The user doesn't need to review grey boxes to benefit.

Previs stills restyled into frames hold geography well. An animated blockout carries timing
and camera paths through an editing route (Seedance 2.5 editing, H3 Max 3D-to-video), but
the model copies it literally, flaws included: stiff proxy animation becomes stiff acting,
a stray prop or a stutter comes back in the take, and a grey puppet can render as a puppet.
Check the proxy before spending; when its motion is the weak part, give the model restyled
stills and keep the animatic only for timing. Smooth dollies and arcs transfer better than
many eased keyframes; whip pans smear. Build proxies for literal copying: one smooth volume
per character in its own flat colour near its real one, flat full lighting, nothing
floating, and the prompt saying the shapes mark only position and motion.

**Restyling the user's footage.** The source carries the camera, timing and performance; a
restyled anchor frame made from it (frame first, style reference second, poses and positions
kept) carries the look. Submit each section with its anchor on an editing route, naming what
stays (camera movement, timing, poses, composition), and
check through the ending, where a take can freeze or revert. To swap in Elements instead,
generating from them with the clip as a motion reference usually holds identity better.

**Matching a reference clip:** `voyager reference download` fetches an online video; find its
cuts with the bundled ffmpeg's `scdet` filter and plan shot lengths and moves against the
measured ones. Ask the user before retrying with their browser cookies (`--browser`).

### Long-form

A film minutes long, a contest or a client piece gets a plan, not a gate, as light as the
piece allows. Keep plain notes in `films/<short-name>/`: story, shot list, look, and per scene
each shot's prompt, inputs and the user's notes, so retakes rebuild from them. When narration
or a song drives the piece, make it first and time the shots to its measured length. A
scene's drafts shown together reveal pacing and continuity cheaply, before the spend of
finishing them; report spend as you go. Before presenting, describe what the cut shows as a
stranger would: a missed turn can sometimes be fixed in the edit, and otherwise needs the
missing shot.

## Writing prompts

Each model's playbook has its structure, and its syntax wins where it differs; these hold for
most models:

- **Starting positions stated**, or models open on an empty frame or re-establish.
- **Detail sets the frame**: hands, props or another person's shoulder in the prompt get that
  much frame, whatever shot size you name.
- **A few clear simultaneous actions**, shown by physical tells, not emotion words.
- **Camera move and subject pace in separate sentences**: speed words leak into everything.
- **Physics stated**: where the light comes from, real-time motion unless slow motion is
  meant, weight, rigid things rigid, idle hands at rest.
- **Two or more people**: a count, relative heights, who stands where and holds what, and
  distinct silhouettes and colours.
- **Only what was asked**, and only this shot's people and props; later characters leak in.
  Anything you added that draws a complaint comes out of prompt and stills.
- **Each reference's role in words**: what it supplies and what to ignore.
- **Models don't know rules or remember exact state**: a game, a score, an instrument's fingering
  or a board position comes out wrong or changes between shots, so frame around the moment that
  would expose it.
- **Sound written**, or the model improvises it; on shots cut under one score, no music.
- **Dialogue directed, not just written.** Punctuation shapes delivery, so write lines the way
  they should be said, with short lines and deliberate pauses; small physical actions between
  lines make delivery feel natural more than any adjective does. Speech, pauses and reactions
  all take clip time, so time dialogue from the script, not a line count.
- **Exact text is unreliable**: logos, prices, claims and UI come out right as overlays or
  authored assets, unless the chosen model renders text well.
- **Exclusions as the wanted state**, outside a model's own negative field: many models drift
  toward what a prompt names.

With `cast`, pass the element IDs and project directory on every estimate and run that shows
them, and write around the labels Voyager returns.

## Generate, check, deliver

Start every generation from what the user approved, never a rejected take, and give each idea
a short title so its takes share a file name. Submit every clip of an approved batch before
waiting on any, and carry an approved plan through to the finished video: a job wait is not a
stopping point. A request identical to an earlier one returns that job (`reused`) and charges
nothing. Voyager handles provider fallback, so a failed job isn't yours to resubmit on another model.
When a content filter refuses an allowed request, say which provider refused, without guessing
a trigger it didn't name. Another model is a new paid generation and, for a model the user
named, their call; rewording rarely gets past a refusal of a face reference, while the
refusal's own suggestions (other models, a stylized Element) often do. Keep the same `cast` IDs; never relabel a card
to get past a refusal.
When a safety refusal carries `accessAlternative` (Wan 3.0 Spicy), it is available for
appropriate violence and non-explicit mature scenes, never for explicit sex, anyone under
18, real or recognizable people, extreme gore or other illegal content. Ask first with the
question tool; never write links, as the app draws the buttons. A refusal from Voyager's
own check on Spicy (`checkedBy: "voyager"`) is final: never retry or reword around it.

Look at every take before the user does. Takes fail in ways a prompt can't prevent: the
shot's action never happens, faces and hands change, objects appear or vanish, text is
invented, people float or swap sides, the model adds its own cuts, and faults often arrive
late, after a good opening. `voyager media review` catches technical faults (black or frozen
frames, silence, a squashed opening), `voyager media frames` gives stills anywhere in the clip,
and [hosted understanding](references/understanding.md) judges motion, sync and sound that
stills can't show. A fault a viewer sees at normal speed is a blocker; one visible only frame
by frame is polish. Fix every blocker before presenting: never present a cut while
naming a problem you could fix ("the earbuds don't match the real product", "the end card
is plain text"). Fix it, review again and repeat, within the budget the user already
authorized; a paid retry beyond it is their call. Only what just the user can supply (their
private assets, a claim to confirm) is asked for, once. A public product's official photos
and logo, a brand's site assets or a well-known place are not that: look them up and use
them as references or composite them first.

Takes of one prompt vary widely, so a single take says little about whether a change worked.
A re-roll gambles everything that was good; trimming, covering, a time-ranged edit or an
extension from an approved opening keeps it. A regenerated shot loses the user's corrections
unless its prompt carries them. Finish kept drafts without losing what was approved (the
model's own draft completion, or an upscale of the kept take or the locked cut); regenerating
at a higher setting makes a new take to approve again. If draft completion is refused,
tell the user the error and ask before upscaling or regenerating that shot; an upscale
never quietly replaces completion. Upscaling and relighting can invent
detail or pump exposure.

Present each draft and the final with `voyager files present` under one deliverable name.
A storyboard is a strip: present each frame as its own deliverable ("Shot 1", "Shot 2") and send
the canvas hint from [canvas-layout](references/canvas-layout.md); character references are a
`reference` grid, and `pick` the take the user chooses.

Cut in the user's chosen editor ([davinci-resolve](../davinci-resolve/SKILL.md),
[premiere-pro](../premiere-pro/SKILL.md), [capcut](../capcut/SKILL.md)); otherwise the video
engine as [edit-video](../edit-video/SKILL.md) describes, when `<voyager_environment>` lists
it as ready; otherwise `voyager media assemble`, never a hand-written FFmpeg concat. Generated
clips tend to open unsteady and drift at the tail.

Each clip's native sound is made alone, so ambience jumps or drops out at every cut unless a
continuous bed runs under them; sound overlapping a cut (J- and L-cuts in `media assemble`)
hides joins. Score: [make-music](../make-music/SKILL.md); effects and mix:
[make-sound](../make-sound/SKILL.md); narration: [voiceover](../voiceover/SKILL.md). Native
speech is accurate for a line or two in one take, and a voice can drift between generations
unless the same references carry it. A chosen or cloned voice, or a presenter reused across
pieces, is voiced first and lip-synced. Most social video plays muted, and vertical feeds
cover parts of the frame ([social safe areas](../edit-video/references/social-safe-areas.md)).

Generated footage must not pass for evidence of a real event; label it as a visualization
where viewers could mistake it.
